Q: Is my method for managing individual event driven tasks in python asyncio overkill? A:

Yes - reading that: it is good. The incorrection is that you should have a finally clause, not an else in your done_callback function: the cancelled tasks remain in the registry in your example code.

No - you have just a registry and a done_callback for each task, that is far from overkill when we talk about asyncio.

If you prefer not to use callbacks, the pattern I normally use is to have a 'monitor' task which is keeps running in a while True loop, and fetches tasks from a queue: the container with all tasks can then be local to this monitor task, and your "task creator" utility function would put the new tasks to this queue instead of in the registry - but in your scenario, I don't think it would be easy for it to work with no done_callbacks either: for one, the monitor task at one point will have to pause and await for one of the tasks it "already have" to finnish - but in your scenario, a task which arrives later could run to completion and never notify anything until at least one task from an earler batch would complete.

That said: having a utility function to create a task, set its callback, and add it to a registry or queue is perfectly correct for asyncio code.

(also, no need for an if and an extra line to set a task name: recent Pythons have the name= parameter directly in asyncio.create_task which defaults to None - and, yes, in your example code, that is another error: the name should be required and unique there, or you would override existing entries in the registry)

Option 2: leveraging taskGroup

Since your pattern wants to always cancel the tasks depending on a resource when it finnishes, you can write those resources themselves as a subclass of Taskgroups: It will simplify your code a bit once you won't have to worry about the cancelation logic.

Also, if you don't need in your "run_coro" inside the resource to address tasks individually, you may skip the registry as well (taskgroups have a "registry" of their own in the ._tasks attribute).

The "task creator wrapper" and "done_callback" are still there - if you don't check explicitly for a class exception there, the whole group will be cancelled on the first task that errors out.

Here is your example above converted to do that:

# Source - https://stackoverflow.com/q/79995450
# Posted by iamthebull
# Retrieved 2026-08-17, License - CC BY-SA 4.0

import sys
import asyncio
import logging
from typing import Coroutine
from functools import partial

logging.basicConfig(level = logging.DEBUG, stream = sys.stdout, format = '%(asctime)s | %(levelname)7s | %(taskName)s | %(message)s')
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

type TaskName = str
type TaskRegistry = dict[TaskName, asyncio.Task]

def task_done_callback(task: asyncio.Task, registry: TaskRegistry):
    logger.info(f"task done callback - {task.get_name()}")
    try:
        exception = task.exception()
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        logger.info(f'task cancelled - {task.get_name()}')
    else:
        if exception:
            logger.info(f"error in task - {exception} - {task.get_name()}")
        logger.info(f"task finished - {task.get_name()}")
        registry.pop(task.get_name())

def create_child_task(coro: Coroutine, registry: TaskRegistry, task_name: TaskName = None, group: asyncio.TaskGroup | None = None) -> asyncio.Task:
    if group is None:
        group = asyncio
    task = group.create_task(coro, name=task_name)
    task.add_done_callback(partial(task_done_callback, registry=registry))
    registry[task.get_name()] = task
    return task

class Resource(asyncio.TaskGroup):

    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        # needed because, at least in this example, you want to manipulate "child task 3" explicitly.
        # if that is not needed in your project, you may not need a parallel task registry
        # in the resource:
        self.child_tasks: TaskRegistry = {}
        super().__init__()

    async def __aenter__(self):
        self.__started = True
        started_self = await super().__aenter__()
        self.__runner = self.create_task(self.run_coro())
        return started_self

    async def __aexit__(self, *args):
        self.__started = False
        self.__runner.cancel()
        return await super().__aexit__(*args)

    async def run_coro(self):
        try:
            logger.info('resource running')
            counter = 0
            while True:
                await asyncio.sleep(1)
                counter += 1
                if counter == 4: self.child_tasks['child task 3'].cancel()
        except Exception as e:
            logger.exception(f'uncaught exception in resource - {e}')
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            logger.info('resource cancelled')
            raise
        finally:
            # await cancel_child_tasks(self.child_tasks)
            logger.info('resource stopped')

    async def do_something(self, index: int, duration: int):
        try:
            logger.info(f'do something {index} started')
            await asyncio.sleep(duration)
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            logger.info(f'do something {index} cancelled')
            raise
        else:
            logger.info(f'do something {index} finished')

    def use_resource(self, index: int, duration: int):
        if not self.__started:
            raise RuntimeError("Resource not running")
        return create_child_task(self.do_something(index, duration), registry= self.child_tasks, task_name= f"{self.name} - child task {index}", group= self)


async def main():
    try:
        tasks: TaskRegistry = {}
        async with Resource('Some Resource') as resource:
            # create_child_task(resource.run_coro(), tasks, 'Some Resource Task')
            resource.use_resource(1, 1)   ### pretend these are called by asynchronous events
            resource.use_resource(2, 2)
            resource.use_resource(3, 6)
            resource.use_resource(4, 7)
            counter = 0
            while True:
                await asyncio.sleep(1)
                counter += 1
                logger.debug(f"main counter: {counter}")
    except Exception as e:
        logger.exception(f'uncaught exception in main - {e}')
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        logger.info(f'main cancelled')
    finally:
        # await cancel_child_tasks(tasks)
        logger.info(f'main finished')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    asyncio.run(main())

(PS: I am not an "oo purist" - I am using the double-underscore prefix just to avoid conflict with eventual TaskGroup inner methods and attributes. As it is, it uses "_entered" - so _started it would have worked by sheer chance)

There is a Pelican extension called yaml-metadata which will allow you to keep the yaml metadata. you might need to replace a few names but it works well.

Q: How to access Response cookies in angular2? A:

The name of the response header you are trying to get is actually Set-Cookie not apsession. So if you did something like res.get("set-cookie") it would return the first header that matched that name. Since you have more than 1, you could do:

let headers: Headers = res.headers;
headers.getAll('set-cookie');

which returns a list of all headers with that name. You could find apsession in there probably.

See:

  • https://angular.io/docs/ts/latest/api/http/index/Headers-class.html

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Response/headers

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Headers

Q: Getting javac to work in the PATH environment variable A:

Javac is sitting in the bin directory contained in the area where your java compiler and interpreter were installed. So, assuming the path to bin is C:.....\bin, type set path=%path%;C:.....\bin at the command prompt.

Q: Django admin: Edit model field with 'editable=False' A:

You should be handling this use case via permissions: only user that have the change permission for a Model are allowed to really change it. These permissions exist by default in Django. You simply need to check them before displaying the form.

They can also be used for finer grained control like only showing certain fields. But that logic has to be implemented by you in your views and templates.

Have a look at: https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/1.11/topics/auth/default/#default-permissions

If you still need to edit non-editable field, have a look at: https://stackoverflow.com/a/44720169/621690

Q: Check if a directory exists in a zip file with Python A:

The best way since Python 3.8 is to use zipfile.Path:

zipfile.Path("archive.zip", "folder/file.txt").exists() # file or folder exists?
zipfile.Path("archive.zip", "folder/file.txt").is_file() # file exists?
zipfile.Path("archive.zip", "folder/").is_dir() # folder exists? (end slash needed)

Here's the 4 different methods explained to help you decide which is best:

Fast (O(1))
zipfile.Path Most modern clean way
getinfo() Needs try-except
NameToInfo Internal dictionary lookup

Slow (O(N))
namelist() Generates a list to search through
